branches.description: Trace the movement from Jacob’s renaming to family, tribes, kingdoms, and later disputed uses.
branches.label: Follow the name

branches.description: Hold tribal fracture, two kingdoms, exile, remnant, gathering, and reunited-house language together.
branches.label: Follow division and return

branches.description: Inspect how Jesus, apostles, letters, and visions address or reuse Israel without flattening local referents.
branches.label: Follow later identity

character.centerRule: Israel remains the center only where the source materially forms, addresses, acts through, judges, gathers, remembers, or disputes the collective people. Jacob, Judah, Ephraim, the northern kingdom, outsiders, later communities, and symbolic visions keep their local identities.

phases.orientation: Jacob receives the name Israel, and family, sons, households, and tribes begin to carry it beyond one person.
phases.title: A name becomes a people

phases.orientation: Israel multiplies under pressure, is named God’s firstborn, leaves Egypt, crosses the sea, and sings after deliverance.
phases.title: A people under Egypt

phases.orientation: Food, direct speech, covenant blood, rebellion, renewal, and glory shape Israel near Sinai.
phases.title: Covenant at the mountain

phases.orientation: Atonement, neighbor love, land, blessing, shared Spirit, fear, rebellion, and failed leadership define communal life.
phases.title: A holy and difficult community

phases.orientation: Judgment, blessing, compromise, inheritance, election, love, covenant, and return are rehearsed before entry.
phases.title: Identity before the land

phases.orientation: Crossing, covenant, corporate guilt, repeated rescue, uneven participation, atrocity, and civil fracture test tribal solidarity.
phases.title: Tribes in the land

phases.orientation: Ark, repentance, kingship, covenant warning, tribal unity, Jerusalem, David’s house, and Temple prayer gather the people.
phases.title: Israel asks for a king

phases.orientation: The royal split, rival worship, prophetic contest, conquest, reform, and exile expose competing uses of Israel’s name.
phases.title: One people becomes two kingdoms

phases.orientation: Prophets address rebellion, election, justice, childhood, comfort, witness, false security, renewed covenant, and a cleansed name.
phases.title: Prophets accuse and promise

phases.orientation: Dry bones, reunited sticks, confession, return, communal memory, praise, and restored nations revisit Israel after catastrophe.
phases.title: Exile, memory, and return

phases.orientation: Later witnesses retell origins, confess failure, resist coercion, endure violence, and dispute Israel’s place among the nations.
phases.title: Israel remembered under later empires

phases.orientation: Gospel witnesses place Jesus amid Israel’s mercy, consolation, tribes, lost sheep, outsiders, judgment, and an Israelite named without deceit.
phases.title: Jesus within Israel’s story

phases.orientation: Acts, letters, and Revelation revisit ancestry, remnant, covenant, identity, inclusion, warning, worship, and the twelve tribes.
phases.title: Israel in apostolic argument and final vision

character.throughline: The trail moves from Jacob’s new name through family and exodus, covenant and land, tribal fracture and kingdom, prophetic accusation and exile, later witness, Jesus, apostolic argument, and final tribal imagery.

leftEvidence.title: Jacob is renamed Israel in a night struggle

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: A mysterious man wrestles Jacob, wounds him, renames him Israel, and blesses him.
points.right: God appears again, repeats the new name, promises nations, kings, and land, and goes up from the place.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Jacob names the place for seeing God face to face and leaves limping.
points.right: Jacob raises a pillar, pours an offering, and names Bethel.

compares.posture: Both passages attach Israel to Jacob, divine encounter, blessing, and a future larger than one man.

rightEvidence.title: God confirms the name Israel at Bethel

compares.tension: Genesis 32 emphasizes struggle and injury; Genesis 35 emphasizes divine speech, nations, kings, and land.
compares.title: The name given in struggle and confirmed in promise

leftEvidence.title: Violence brings shame upon Jacob’s household

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Dinah is violated, Shechem seeks marriage, Jacob’s sons answer deceitfully, and Simeon and Levi kill the city’s males.
points.right: Joseph reports on his brothers, receives a special garment, tells dreams, and is sent by Israel to seek the brothers’ welfare.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Jacob fears the surrounding peoples while the brothers defend their sister.
points.right: love, hatred, jealousy, and paternal concern gather around the same household.

compares.posture: Both scenes expose how the actions of Jacob’s sons shape the public and internal future of the family called Israel.

rightEvidence.title: Israel sends Joseph to his brothers

compares.tension: One crisis turns outward through vengeance against a city; the other turns inward through hatred around Joseph.
compares.title: A household threatened by its own sons

leftEvidence.title: Israel descends to Egypt after hearing God

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Israel sacrifices at Beersheba, God addresses Jacob in night visions, and the household travels to Egypt.
points.right: The source names Jacob’s descendants by mothers, sons, daughters, and households and totals those entering Egypt.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: the promise names both a great nation in Egypt and a future return.
points.right: one family is already described through the collective label children of Israel.

compares.posture: The night vision authorizes the move while the genealogy names who carries the family into Egypt.

rightEvidence.title: A household is counted as the children of Israel

compares.tension: Promise speaks of a great nation; the list still presents a bounded household.
compares.title: A promised descent and a counted household

leftEvidence.title: Israel gives Joseph’s sons a place among his own

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Israel claims Ephraim and Manasseh as his, crosses his hands, places the younger before the older, and blesses them.
points.right: Jacob summons his sons, speaks distinct futures over them, and the narrator names them as the twelve tribes of Israel.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Joseph objects, but Israel insists that both will become peoples.
points.right: praise, rebuke, violence, rule, land, abundance, and danger are not distributed evenly.

compares.posture: Israel’s treatment of Joseph’s sons and Jacob’s final sayings both configure the later tribal people.

rightEvidence.title: Israel speaks over the tribes before his death

compares.tension: One act gives Joseph two tribal lines; the final speech assigns different memories and futures to the sons.
compares.title: Adoption and the shape of the tribes

leftEvidence.title: The children of Israel multiply under oppression

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: A family list opens into a numerous people, a new king fears them, and forced labor and death orders intensify.
points.right: The children of Israel groan, cry, and sigh under bondage.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: the more Israel is afflicted, the more the people multiply and spread.
points.right: God hears, remembers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, sees the people, and knows.

compares.posture: Oppression grows as Israel multiplies, and the next source answers groaning with divine covenant attention.

rightEvidence.title: God hears Israel and remembers covenant

compares.tension: Exodus 1 foregrounds imperial fear and policy; Exodus 2 foregrounds Israel’s cry and God’s response.
compares.title: A multiplied people becomes a heard people

leftEvidence.title: Israel’s affliction leads to Moses’ commission

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: The LORD says Israel’s affliction is seen and its cry heard, promises descent and deliverance, and sends Moses to Pharaoh.
points.right: The LORD tells Moses what to say to Pharaoh and names Israel as son and firstborn.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Moses asks who he is and what divine name he should give the people.
points.right: refusal to release that son is answered with a threat against Pharaoh’s firstborn.

compares.posture: Moses’ commission and the firstborn declaration interpret the confrontation with Pharaoh through relationship as well as liberation.

rightEvidence.title: Israel is called God’s son and firstborn

compares.tension: One passage stresses seen suffering and a sent messenger; the other compresses sonship, demand, refusal, and threatened death.
compares.title: A suffering people named as a son

leftEvidence.title: Marked Israelite houses are passed over

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Israelite households mark doors with blood and remain inside while Egypt’s firstborn die.
points.right: The Egyptians urge departure, the people carry unleavened dough and requested goods, and a mixed multitude goes with them.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Pharaoh summons Moses and orders Israel to leave.
points.right: the night is kept as a vigil for the LORD.

compares.posture: The Passover protects marked houses, and the departure gathers those houses into movement with others.

rightEvidence.title: Israel leaves Egypt with a mixed company

compares.tension: Household boundaries are precise during the night; the departing multitude is socially wider.
compares.title: Protected households become a departing company

leftEvidence.title: Israel fears, crosses, and sees Egypt defeated

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Israel cries out at the approaching army, Moses calls for stillness, the sea opens, and the people cross on dry ground.
points.right: Moses and the children of Israel sing of the LORD’s triumph, power, holiness, guidance, and future sanctuary.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Israel sees the Egyptians dead and fears and believes the LORD.
points.right: Miriam and the women answer with percussion and dance.

compares.posture: The narrative tells what Israel sees at the sea, while the song tells the people how to remember its meaning.

rightEvidence.title: Israel sings after the sea

compares.tension: Fear and belief close the narrative; kingship, sanctuary, nations, and future land expand the song.
compares.title: Deliverance experienced and interpreted

leftEvidence.title: Israel receives bread and a daily test

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: The congregation complains about hunger, the LORD promises bread, and manna appears with instructions for daily gathering.
points.right: At Sinai the LORD recalls carrying Israel from Egypt and proposes covenant obedience, treasured possession, priestly kingdom, and holy nation.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: unequal gathering results in enough for each person.
points.right: the people answer together that they will do all spoken words.

compares.posture: Daily food and Sinai identity both define a people learning dependence and obedience.

rightEvidence.title: Israel is called a treasured possession and priestly kingdom

compares.tension: Manna gives enough under repeated instruction; the mountain names a holy, priestly vocation before the people’s later failures.
compares.title: Provision before covenant vocation

leftEvidence.title: Israel hears the covenant words and stands far off

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: God speaks words concerning worship, name, Sabbath, family, life, marriage, property, testimony, and desire.
points.right: Moses records the words, the people twice promise obedience, blood is placed on altar and people, and representatives ascend, see Israel’s God, and eat and drink.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: thunder, lightning, trumpet, and smoke leave the people afraid and at a distance.

compares.posture: Israel receives direct words and then enters a blood-marked covenant represented by leaders who see and eat.

rightEvidence.title: Israel enters covenant through words, blood, and a meal

compares.tension: The people stand far off in fear, while representatives later ascend and survive the meal.
compares.title: Words heard at a distance and covenant sealed in nearness

leftEvidence.title: Israel makes a calf while Moses is on the mountain

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: The people demand gods, Aaron makes a calf, and the celebration names it as the one that brought Israel from Egypt.
points.right: Moses breaks the tablets, destroys the calf, confronts Aaron, and the Levites kill within the camp.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: God speaks of destruction, while Moses appeals to deliverance, reputation, and ancestral promise.
points.right: Moses then seeks atonement and offers himself, but the LORD distinguishes the sinner and sends a plague.

compares.posture: The first passage carries Moses’ appeal; the second returns him to the object, Aaron, the camp, and unresolved consequence.

rightEvidence.title: Broken tablets, violence, and intercession follow the calf

compares.tension: Relenting from total destruction does not prevent broken tablets, deaths, plague, or further intercession.
compares.title: The calf defended before God and judged in the camp

leftEvidence.title: Covenant renewal begins with the divine name

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Moses cuts new tablets, the LORD descends and proclaims mercy, grace, patience, covenant love, forgiveness, and judgment.
points.right: The cloud covers the tent, glory fills the tabernacle, and even Moses cannot enter.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Moses asks that the stiff-necked people be taken as an inheritance.
points.right: Israel moves only when the cloud lifts, with fire visible at night.

compares.posture: Renewal declares divine character, and the completed tabernacle makes divine presence visible throughout Israel’s travel.

rightEvidence.title: Glory fills the dwelling and guides Israel

compares.tension: Mercy and judgment are spoken in one scene; access and exclusion are enacted through cloud and glory in the other.
compares.title: A proclaimed name and a dwelling presence

leftEvidence.title: Atonement cleanses people, priests, and sanctuary

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: After the deaths of Aaron’s sons, guarded entry, sacrifices, blood, confession, and the live goat address impurity and sin.
points.right: The whole congregation is told to be holy through family honor, Sabbath, worship, provision for poor and foreigner, honest judgment, truthful speech, and love of neighbor.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: the rite reaches priest, people, altar, tent, and holy place.
points.right: holiness is not confined to ritual space.

compares.posture: Leviticus places guarded annual atonement beside holiness practiced through ordinary social obligations.

rightEvidence.title: Holiness reaches fields, courts, speech, and neighbors

compares.tension: One passage concentrates ritual mediation; the other addresses the whole congregation’s fields, courts, speech, and relationships.
compares.title: Cleansing the sanctuary and living holiness in public

leftEvidence.title: Israel’s land rests and returns

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: The land receives Sabbath, liberty is proclaimed in the jubilee, property returns, and prices reflect remaining years.
points.right: Aaron and his sons are given words of blessing for the children of Israel, naming protection, favor, grace, attention, and peace.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Israel is told the land belongs to the LORD and the people are resident foreigners.
points.right: the LORD says this places the divine name on the people.

compares.posture: Jubilee limits ownership, and priestly blessing places the divine name on the people.

rightEvidence.title: The divine name is placed on Israel in blessing

compares.tension: Israel is called resident foreigner regarding land while also receiving named favor, protection, and peace.
compares.title: A people living on God’s land under God’s name

leftEvidence.title: Complaint leads to shared leadership and Spirit

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Craving and lament overwhelm Moses, who asks why he carries the people alone.
points.right: The spies agree that the land is fruitful but divide over whether Israel can enter.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: seventy elders receive the Spirit, including two in the camp, and Moses wishes all the LORD’s people were prophets.
points.right: the congregation weeps, proposes returning to Egypt, and threatens Joshua and Caleb.

compares.posture: One crisis widens Spirit-enabled leadership; the other shows an assembly united by fear against faithful witnesses.

rightEvidence.title: The assembly chooses fear after seeing the land

compares.tension: Communal participation can carry provision or amplify unbelief.
compares.title: Shared leadership and shared refusal

leftEvidence.title: Pardon does not remove the wilderness sentence

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: The LORD threatens destruction, Moses appeals to reputation and proclaimed character, and the people are pardoned.
points.right: The congregation disputes with Moses and Aaron, the LORD gives instructions, and water comes from the rock.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: the unbelieving generation nevertheless receives years in the wilderness and exclusion from the land.
points.right: Moses and Aaron are told they did not believe or sanctify the LORD before Israel.

compares.posture: The spies crisis sentences a generation, and Meribah bars Moses and Aaron while still supplying water.

rightEvidence.title: Israel receives water while leaders fail to honor God

compares.tension: Pardon and provision coexist with consequences that reach both people and leaders.
compares.title: A generation excluded and leaders excluded

leftEvidence.title: Israel confesses after speaking against God and Moses

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Impatience becomes accusation, fiery serpents bring death, and the people confess and ask for intercession.
points.right: Balak builds altars and Balaam seeks a word, but the oracle asks how one can curse whom God has not cursed.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: the LORD commands a bronze serpent, and looking becomes the means of living.
points.right: Israel is viewed as a people dwelling apart and too numerous to count.

compares.posture: A camp under judgment receives a life-giving sign, while an outsider hired to curse sees a blessed and numerous people.

rightEvidence.title: A hired curse becomes blessing over Israel

compares.tension: One source centers confession and danger within Israel; the other centers a resistant oracle outside Israel.
compares.title: Israel seen through judgment and outsider blessing

leftEvidence.title: Israel joins Baal of Peor and faces plague

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Sexual relations, sacrificial meals, and attachment to Baal bring anger and death.
points.right: Five women name their father, his death, lack of sons, and risk of losing his name.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Phinehas kills an Israelite man and Midianite woman and receives a covenant of peace and priesthood.
points.right: Moses brings their case before the LORD, and their claim becomes a statute for Israel.

compares.posture: One scene answers a communal crisis through lethal zeal; another answers a family vulnerability through heard petition and new statute.

rightEvidence.title: The daughters of Zelophehad change Israel’s inheritance law

compares.tension: Both change Israel’s future practice, but through radically different forms of agency.
compares.title: Zeal and legal hearing before the land

leftEvidence.title: Israel’s life and law are displayed before nations

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Moses calls Israel to hear and live, recalls Baal Peor, and says faithful practice will appear as wisdom to other peoples.
points.right: Israel is commanded to hear, love the LORD with the whole self, keep words in the heart, teach children, and mark ordinary spaces and routines.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: the mountain voice gives words but no visible form.
points.right: covenant identity is carried through repeated embodied memory.

compares.posture: Deuteronomy links Israel’s law to national witness and to daily love taught across generations.

rightEvidence.title: Israel hears one LORD and learns daily remembrance

compares.tension: Nations observe enacted wisdom; children receive repeated words in domestic life.
compares.title: Public wisdom and household remembrance

leftEvidence.title: Israel is chosen despite being few

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Israel is called holy and treasured, but election is explicitly denied a basis in size.
points.right: Moses binds leaders, children, foreigners, and absent generations into covenant, warns of exile, and anticipates return and heart transformation.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: love, oath, deliverance, covenant faithfulness, and judgment frame the choice.
points.right: life and death are set before Israel as a present choice.

compares.posture: Election is grounded in love and oath, while the later covenant anticipates exile, return, heart change, and renewed choice.

rightEvidence.title: Covenant includes hidden things, exile, return, and choice

compares.tension: Chosen identity does not remove judgment, and promised return does not eliminate commanded response.
compares.title: Election before failure and return after failure

leftEvidence.title: Moses gives Israel a song that will testify against them

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Moses calls heaven and earth to hear a song that names God faithful, Israel corrupt, election unearned, apostasy foreseeable, and judgment severe.
points.right: Elders come to inquire, but the prophetic speech retells rebellion in Egypt, wilderness, and land, repeatedly saying action was taken for the divine name.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: the song also refuses final abandonment and Moses tells the people to set their hearts on its words.
points.right: future gathering includes judgment, remembered shame, and renewed service.

compares.posture: Moses gives Israel a song that anticipates corruption and testifies across generations; Ezekiel retells rebellion in Egypt, wilderness, and land while centering the divine name.

rightEvidence.title: Ezekiel retells Israel’s rebellions and God’s name

compares.tension: Both sources interpret Israel’s whole story, but one stands before entry and the other addresses elders after accumulated failure.
compares.title: A witness song and a prophetic history of rebellion

leftEvidence.title: All Israel crosses the Jordan on dry ground

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: The ark goes before the people, the waters stop, priests stand in the riverbed, and all Israel crosses.
points.right: Joshua circumcises those born in the wilderness, Israel remains at Gilgal until healing, Passover is kept, produce of the land is eaten, and manna ceases.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Joshua’s public leadership is confirmed in a scene echoing the sea.

compares.posture: The crossing brings all Israel into the land, and Gilgal pauses the people for circumcision, Passover, and new food.

rightEvidence.title: A wilderness generation is circumcised before Passover

compares.tension: Public movement precedes bodily sign and household feast; manna then ceases.
compares.title: Entry through water and entry through covenant memory

leftEvidence.title: One hidden act brings defeat upon Israel

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Achan takes devoted property, Israel loses at Ai, and investigation narrows from people to tribe, clan, household, and person.
points.right: Joshua recounts ancestors, exodus, wilderness, land, and defeated kings, then calls for exclusive service.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Achan’s household and possessions are destroyed with him.
points.right: the people choose the LORD, Joshua warns they cannot serve, and covenant testimony is established.

compares.posture: Achan’s act is attributed to Israel, while Shechem gathers all Israel to rehearse history and promise service.

rightEvidence.title: Israel rehearses its story and chooses whom to serve

compares.tension: Corporate guilt narrows to one household; corporate commitment is spoken by an assembly whose future will fracture.
compares.title: One hidden breach and one public pledge

leftEvidence.title: A generation forgets and a cycle begins

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: After Joshua’s generation dies, Israel serves other gods, faces plunderers, cries under oppression, receives judges, and turns back after each judge dies.
points.right: Deborah and Barak sing of willing leaders and people, the LORD’s march, tribal participation, hesitation, absence, Jael’s act, and Sisera’s waiting mother.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: the nations remain as a test.
points.right: Israel’s unity is praised and questioned in one poem.

compares.posture: The Judges summary describes a repeated national cycle, while Deborah’s song names particular tribes that came or stayed.

rightEvidence.title: A victory song names tribes that came and tribes that stayed

compares.tension: The collective label Israel can conceal sharply different tribal responses.
compares.title: Recurring rescue and uneven tribal participation

leftEvidence.title: An atrocity is sent throughout Israel

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Men surround the house, a woman is handed over, abused, and dies, and her body is divided and sent through Israel.
points.right: An oath against Benjamin creates grief over a missing tribe, and Israel answers through killing at Jabesh Gilead and abducting women at Shiloh.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: recipients say such a thing has not happened since Egypt.
points.right: the book ends by saying there was no king and everyone did what was right in his own eyes.

compares.posture: The Gibeah atrocity mobilizes Israel, and the aftermath seeks to preserve Benjamin through more killings and abductions.

rightEvidence.title: Israel tries to preserve Benjamin through further violence

compares.tension: Collective outrage does not prevent collective actions that repeat disregard for vulnerable lives.
compares.title: Violence exposed and violence multiplied

leftEvidence.title: Israel brings the ark into battle and loses it

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: After defeat, Israel brings the ark from Shiloh expecting rescue, the camp shouts, and the Philistines fear.
points.right: Samuel calls for wholehearted return, Israel removes Baals and Ashtaroth, confesses, and asks for intercession.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Israel is defeated again, Eli’s sons die, and the ark is captured.
points.right: the LORD thunders against the Philistines, and Samuel sets a stone of help.

compares.posture: Israel first carries the ark as a guarantee, then later removes foreign gods, confesses, and asks for intercession.

rightEvidence.title: Israel removes foreign gods and gathers at Mizpah

compares.tension: Defeat follows attempted control; deliverance follows a broader reorientation that still includes battle and memorial.
compares.title: Sacred object and covenant return

leftEvidence.title: Israel asks for a king like the nations

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: The elders cite Samuel’s sons and ask for a king to judge them, and the LORD interprets the request as rejection.
points.right: Samuel calls down thunder during wheat harvest, the people fear and confess asking for a king, and Samuel tells them not to turn aside.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Samuel warns about royal taking, but the people insist on visible rule and warfare.
points.right: he also calls ceasing to pray for them a sin.

compares.posture: Samuel warns before kingship and later confirms the people’s wrongdoing after a king exists.

rightEvidence.title: Thunder exposes Israel’s request, but covenant service remains open

compares.tension: Permission does not turn the request into innocence, yet covenant service remains open.
compares.title: A king granted and a request exposed

leftEvidence.title: All Israel’s tribes anoint David king

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: The tribes name kinship, David’s earlier leadership, and the LORD’s shepherd promise, and the elders make covenant with him.
points.right: David brings the ark with sacrifice, dancing, shouting, and trumpet, blesses the people, and distributes food.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: David becomes king over all Israel after ruling Judah separately.
points.right: Michal despises him and their dispute closes the scene.

compares.posture: All tribes covenant with David, and the ark’s entry gives Jerusalem a national worship role.

rightEvidence.title: David brings the ark into Jerusalem with celebration

compares.tension: Public unity and celebration coexist with prior conflict and household contempt.
compares.title: Tribal unity and a new royal center

leftEvidence.title: God promises Israel a place and David a house

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: The oracle recalls taking David from pasture, promises a name, a planted place for Israel, rest from enemies, and a dynastic house.
points.right: At the Temple Solomon names covenant, sin, defeat, drought, famine, foreign prayer, war, captivity, forgiveness, justice, and return.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: discipline and enduring covenant love remain part of the promise.
points.right: he denies that heaven can contain God while asking God to hear toward the house.

compares.posture: David’s oracle links dynasty and Israel’s planted place, while Solomon’s prayer addresses God from the Temple and imagines exile.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon prays for Israel, foreigners, and future exiles

compares.tension: Neither dynasty nor sanctuary guarantees unbroken national security.
compares.title: A promised house and a praying house

leftEvidence.title: The kingdom divides after Rehoboam answers harshly

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: All Israel asks for lighter service, Rehoboam rejects elder counsel, and ten tribes make Jeroboam king while Judah remains with David’s house.
points.right: Fearing return to David’s house, Jeroboam builds calves at Bethel and Dan, changes priesthood and festival, and presents the images as the gods who brought Israel from Egypt.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: the prophet stops an attempted civil war by naming the division as from the LORD.
points.right: political security reshapes worship.

compares.posture: The split gives Jeroboam a kingdom, and his fear of losing it produces rival worship centers and an altered calendar.

rightEvidence.title: Jeroboam creates rival worship for Israel

compares.tension: A division named within divine purpose becomes the setting for human manipulation of Israel’s worship memory.
compares.title: Political division and religious redesign

leftEvidence.title: Elijah asks Israel how long it will limp between claims

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Ahab gathers Israel and Baal’s prophets, Elijah demands a choice, two sacrifices are prepared, and fire answers Elijah’s prayer.
points.right: Samaria is captured and Israel exiled, and the narrator reviews idolatry, rejected warnings, covenant breach, imitation of nations, and child sacrifice.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: the people confess the LORD before the prophets of Baal are killed.
points.right: Judah is also named as failing.

compares.posture: Carmel ends with Israel confessing the LORD, while Kings later explains northern exile through sustained covenant refusal.

rightEvidence.title: The northern kingdom falls after a long indictment

compares.tension: One dramatic sign does not produce durable national change.
compares.title: Public confession and long-term exile

leftEvidence.title: Hezekiah’s trust is narrated beside Israel’s exile

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: Hezekiah removes high places and the bronze serpent, trusts the LORD, and prospers.
points.right: The book of the law is found, read to Josiah, and tears his clothes.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: the account then repeats Samaria’s fall for failure to hear and obey covenant.
points.right: Huldah confirms announced disaster while granting the king a peaceful death because he humbled himself.

compares.posture: Hezekiah destroys a former wilderness sign turned idol, and Josiah is pierced by words no longer practiced.

rightEvidence.title: A found book exposes Judah’s distance from covenant

compares.tension: Both reforms recover covenant loyalty by refusing to preserve a sacred object or institution in the wrong way.
compares.title: Reform through remembered signs and rediscovered words

leftEvidence.title: Josiah gathers Judah and Israel’s remnant for covenant renewal

points.label: Israel setting and claim
points.left: The king reads the covenant, the people stand to it, and worship sites, objects, priests, mediums, and Passover practices are reformed across Judah and former northern territory.
points.right: Zedekiah rebels, Babylon besieges Jerusalem, famine intensifies, the king is captured, sons are killed, eyes are put out, Temple and city are burned, and people are exiled.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Josiah is praised for whole-hearted return.
points.right: only some poor remain.

edges.basis: Both passages attach Israel to Jacob, divine encounter, blessing, and a future larger than one man. Genesis 32 emphasizes struggle and injury; Genesis 35 emphasizes divine speech, nations, kings, and land.
edges.label: The name given in struggle and confirmed in promise

edges.basis: Both scenes expose how the actions of Jacob’s sons shape the public and internal future of the family called Israel. One crisis turns outward through vengeance against a city; the other turns inward through hatred around Joseph.
edges.label: A household threatened by its own sons

edges.basis: The night vision authorizes the move while the genealogy names who carries the family into Egypt. Promise speaks of a great nation; the list still presents a bounded household.
edges.label: A promised descent and a counted household

edges.basis: Israel’s treatment of Joseph’s sons and Jacob’s final sayings both configure the later tribal people. One act gives Joseph two tribal lines; the final speech assigns different memories and futures to the sons.
edges.label: Adoption and the shape of the tribes

edges.basis: Oppression grows as Israel multiplies, and the next source answers groaning with divine covenant attention. Exodus 1 foregrounds imperial fear and policy; Exodus 2 foregrounds Israel’s cry and God’s response.
edges.label: A multiplied people becomes a heard people

edges.basis: Moses’ commission and the firstborn declaration interpret the confrontation with Pharaoh through relationship as well as liberation. One passage stresses seen suffering and a sent messenger; the other compresses sonship, demand, refusal, and threatened death.
edges.label: A suffering people named as a son

edges.basis: The Passover protects marked houses, and the departure gathers those houses into movement with others. Household boundaries are precise during the night; the departing multitude is socially wider.
edges.label: Protected households become a departing company

edges.basis: The narrative tells what Israel sees at the sea, while the song tells the people how to remember its meaning. Fear and belief close the narrative; kingship, sanctuary, nations, and future land expand the song.
edges.label: Deliverance experienced and interpreted

edges.basis: Daily food and Sinai identity both define a people learning dependence and obedience. Manna gives enough under repeated instruction; the mountain names a holy, priestly vocation before the people’s later failures.
edges.label: Provision before covenant vocation

edges.basis: Israel receives direct words and then enters a blood-marked covenant represented by leaders who see and eat. The people stand far off in fear, while representatives later ascend and survive the meal.
edges.label: Words heard at a distance and covenant sealed in nearness

edges.basis: The first passage carries Moses’ appeal; the second returns him to the object, Aaron, the camp, and unresolved consequence. Relenting from total destruction does not prevent broken tablets, deaths, plague, or further intercession.
edges.label: The calf defended before God and judged in the camp

edges.basis: Renewal declares divine character, and the completed tabernacle makes divine presence visible throughout Israel’s travel. Mercy and judgment are spoken in one scene; access and exclusion are enacted through cloud and glory in the other.
edges.label: A proclaimed name and a dwelling presence

edges.basis: Leviticus places guarded annual atonement beside holiness practiced through ordinary social obligations. One passage concentrates ritual mediation; the other addresses the whole congregation’s fields, courts, speech, and relationships.
edges.label: Cleansing the sanctuary and living holiness in public

edges.basis: Jubilee limits ownership, and priestly blessing places the divine name on the people. Israel is called resident foreigner regarding land while also receiving named favor, protection, and peace.
edges.label: A people living on God’s land under God’s name

edges.basis: One crisis widens Spirit-enabled leadership; the other shows an assembly united by fear against faithful witnesses. Communal participation can carry provision or amplify unbelief.
edges.label: Shared leadership and shared refusal

edges.basis: The spies crisis sentences a generation, and Meribah bars Moses and Aaron while still supplying water. Pardon and provision coexist with consequences that reach both people and leaders.
edges.label: A generation excluded and leaders excluded

edges.basis: A camp under judgment receives a life-giving sign, while an outsider hired to curse sees a blessed and numerous people. One source centers confession and danger within Israel; the other centers a resistant oracle outside Israel.
edges.label: Israel seen through judgment and outsider blessing

edges.basis: One scene answers a communal crisis through lethal zeal; another answers a family vulnerability through heard petition and new statute. Both change Israel’s future practice, but through radically different forms of agency.
edges.label: Zeal and legal hearing before the land

edges.basis: Deuteronomy links Israel’s law to national witness and to daily love taught across generations. Nations observe enacted wisdom; children receive repeated words in domestic life.
edges.label: Public wisdom and household remembrance

edges.basis: Election is grounded in love and oath, while the later covenant anticipates exile, return, heart change, and renewed choice. Chosen identity does not remove judgment, and promised return does not eliminate commanded response.
edges.label: Election before failure and return after failure

edges.basis: Moses gives Israel a song that anticipates corruption and testifies across generations; Ezekiel retells rebellion in Egypt, wilderness, and land while centering the divine name. Both sources interpret Israel’s whole story, but one stands before entry and the other addresses elders after accumulated failure.
edges.label: A witness song and a prophetic history of rebellion

edges.basis: The crossing brings all Israel into the land, and Gilgal pauses the people for circumcision, Passover, and new food. Public movement precedes bodily sign and household feast; manna then ceases.
edges.label: Entry through water and entry through covenant memory

edges.basis: Achan’s act is attributed to Israel, while Shechem gathers all Israel to rehearse history and promise service. Corporate guilt narrows to one household; corporate commitment is spoken by an assembly whose future will fracture.
edges.label: One hidden breach and one public pledge

edges.basis: The Judges summary describes a repeated national cycle, while Deborah’s song names particular tribes that came or stayed. The collective label Israel can conceal sharply different tribal responses.
edges.label: Recurring rescue and uneven tribal participation

edges.basis: The Gibeah atrocity mobilizes Israel, and the aftermath seeks to preserve Benjamin through more killings and abductions. Collective outrage does not prevent collective actions that repeat disregard for vulnerable lives.
edges.label: Violence exposed and violence multiplied

edges.basis: Israel first carries the ark as a guarantee, then later removes foreign gods, confesses, and asks for intercession. Defeat follows attempted control; deliverance follows a broader reorientation that still includes battle and memorial.
edges.label: Sacred object and covenant return

edges.basis: Samuel warns before kingship and later confirms the people’s wrongdoing after a king exists. Permission does not turn the request into innocence, yet covenant service remains open.
edges.label: A king granted and a request exposed

edges.basis: All tribes covenant with David, and the ark’s entry gives Jerusalem a national worship role. Public unity and celebration coexist with prior conflict and household contempt.
edges.label: Tribal unity and a new royal center

edges.basis: David’s oracle links dynasty and Israel’s planted place, while Solomon’s prayer addresses God from the Temple and imagines exile. Neither dynasty nor sanctuary guarantees unbroken national security.
edges.label: A promised house and a praying house

edges.basis: The split gives Jeroboam a kingdom, and his fear of losing it produces rival worship centers and an altered calendar. A division named within divine purpose becomes the setting for human manipulation of Israel’s worship memory.
edges.label: Political division and religious redesign

edges.basis: Carmel ends with Israel confessing the LORD, while Kings later explains northern exile through sustained covenant refusal. One dramatic sign does not produce durable national change.
edges.label: Public confession and long-term exile

edges.basis: Hezekiah destroys a former wilderness sign turned idol, and Josiah is pierced by words no longer practiced. Both reforms recover covenant loyalty by refusing to preserve a sacred object or institution in the wrong way.
edges.label: Reform through remembered signs and rediscovered words

edges.basis: Josiah’s reform reaches Judah and former Israelite territory, yet Babylon later dismantles kingdom, Temple, and city. Sincere reform changes a generation without erasing accumulated judgment or later royal rebellion.
edges.label: The widest reform before the final fall

edges.basis: Isaiah begins with rebellion and rejected worship, while the later proclamation announces comfort and shepherd care. The same prophetic book refuses both cheap security and permanent abandonment.
edges.label: Children accused and a people comforted

edges.basis: Isaiah names Israel as gathered witness, while Jeremiah confronts people using the Temple to hide injustice. Chosen testimony cannot be separated from the conduct that the people’s worship denies.
edges.label: A redeemed witness and a falsely secure worshiper

edges.basis: Isaiah names a servant Israel who must bring Jacob back, while Hosea gives children names denying mercy and peoplehood before promising reunion. Each source makes Israel both the named subject and the one needing restoration, but through different speakers, figures, and historical pressures.
edges.label: Israel named through restoration and rejected peoplehood

edges.basis: Jeremiah’s gathering imagery centers Ephraim and vulnerable travelers, then promises a new covenant to Israel and Judah. Restoration joins emotional return, reunited houses, transformed instruction, and forgiveness without erasing their names.
edges.label: A gathered firstborn and renewed houses

edges.basis: Hosea and Amos both begin from exodus-shaped relationship and move toward severe accountability. Hosea emphasizes parental compassion; Amos emphasizes election as the reason punishment comes.
edges.label: Loved child and specially known family

edges.basis: Ezekiel 36 promises cleansing, heart, and Spirit, while Ezekiel 37 joins Judah and Joseph under one king and sanctuary. Personal and communal transformation are distinct and mutually related.
edges.label: Inner renewal and reunited public identity

edges.basis: The bones vision pictures lost hope receiving life; Daniel’s prayer takes responsibility for the history leading to exile. Promise of restoration does not bypass confession, and confession does not create life by its own power.
edges.label: National death and communal confession

edges.basis: Cyrus enables return and restores vessels, but Ezra later confesses trespass after a brief period of favor. Return from exile does not complete Israel’s moral restoration.
edges.label: A restored remnant faces new unfaithfulness

edges.basis: Nehemiah’s assembly and Psalm 78 both retell Israel to shape present response. One leads to a written covenant under foreign rule; the other leads toward Judah and David through warning to children.
edges.label: National history as confession and instruction

edges.basis: Psalms 105 and 106 traverse overlapping history from opposed angles. One foregrounds faithful providence and gift; the other foregrounds repeated communal failure and need for gathering.
edges.label: Promise remembered and rebellion confessed

edges.basis: Achior explains Israel to an enemy, while Baruch’s prayer voices guilt from within the dispersed community. The outsider offers a compressed moral pattern; the insiders distribute shame across generations and roles.
edges.label: Israel’s history told by an outsider and by exiles

edges.basis: The decree attacks identity practices, and Mattathias answers by refusing, killing, and fleeing. The sources praise resistance but preserve the morally severe means by which revolt begins.
edges.label: Imperial sameness and violent resistance

edges.basis: Two martyr traditions place national identity in the speech and endurance of mothers and sons. Second Maccabees foregrounds resurrection and judgment; Fourth Maccabees foregrounds reason, formation, and chastity.
edges.label: Israelite identity spoken under torture

edges.basis: One narrative shows an empire attempting mass killing; the other prayer asks why chosen Israel remains dispossessed among nations. Providential rescue and exclusive rhetoric arise from different crises and cannot be collapsed into one rule about nations.
edges.label: A threatened people and a distressed claim over the world

edges.basis: Zechariah and Tobit picture Jerusalem restored and nations drawn toward Israel’s God from different historical settings. Zechariah addresses a rebuilding community in the land; Tobit sings from diaspora about confession, mercy, gathering, and a future city.
edges.label: Restored Jerusalem imagined from land and diaspora

edges.basis: Mary, Simeon, and Anna place Jesus’ birth within mercy to Israel, Abrahamic promise, consolation, and Jerusalem’s redemption. Mary sings before the birth; Simeon and Anna interpret the child while also naming nations and future opposition.
edges.label: Promise remembered and consolation awaited

edges.basis: Matthew applies Israel-shaped texts to Jesus’ childhood and later restricts the Twelve’s first mission to Israel. One passage concentrates national memory in one child; the other sends followers among a scattered people.
edges.label: Israel’s Scripture around Jesus and a mission to Israel

edges.basis: The Canaanite woman presses against an Israel-first mission, while the disciples receive a promise involving Israel’s tribes. Access through persistent appeal and future tribal judgment place Israel’s boundary and destiny under different pressures.
edges.label: An outsider at the boundary and the future of twelve tribes

edges.basis: Matthew targets unfruitful leaders, while John gives a positive and surprising Israelite designation to Nathanael. Israel-related language is not uniformly condemnation or approval; local person, claim, and evidence matter.
edges.label: Judged leaders and an Israelite praised by Jesus

edges.basis: Luke’s disciples describe disappointed hope after the crucifixion, and Acts’ disciples ask about Israel’s kingdom after the resurrection. Jesus redirects both conversations through Scripture, witness, Spirit, or timing without giving a single compact definition of restored Israel.
edges.label: Israel’s redemption hoped for and kingdom restoration asked about

edges.basis: Peter and Paul retell David and Jesus to Israelite audiences after resurrection. Peter directly implicates Jerusalem hearers; Paul addresses Israelites and God-fearers through a longer national history.
edges.label: Israel addressed through resurrection proclamation

edges.basis: Paul claims Israelite ancestry in one letter and grieves while distinguishing Israel within Israel in another. Personal ancestry remains meaningful even as Romans denies that physical descent alone resolves the promise question.
edges.label: Paul’s Israelite identity and his distinction within Israel

edges.basis: Romans and Galatians use compressed Israel language within different arguments about mercy, Gentiles, circumcision, and new creation. Neither phrase defines itself exhaustively, and one letter cannot silently settle the other’s grammar.
edges.label: All Israel and the Israel of God

edges.basis: Ephesians addresses people once outside Israel’s commonwealth, while Philippians presents Paul’s Israelite credentials as real gains he refuses to use as grounds of confidence. One passage names exclusion overcome through nearness; the other names inherited advantage surrendered for Christ.
edges.label: Alienation from Israel and confidence in Israelite ancestry

edges.basis: Hebrews quotes a covenant with Israel and Judah, while 1 Peter applies priestly and people language to dispersed readers. Continuity is explicit, but the sources use different forms of address and do not narrate a simple identity replacement.
edges.label: Israel’s covenant and titles in later communities

edges.basis: Revelation numbers tribes beside a multinational multitude and later inscribes tribal names on the city’s gates. Tribal identity remains symbolically present within visions whose worshipers and citizens come from all nations.
edges.label: Israel’s tribes in the final visions

pivots.description: Jacob receives the name Israel, and family, sons, households, and tribes begin to carry it beyond one person.

nodes.note: A mysterious man wrestles Jacob, wounds him, renames him Israel, and blesses him.

nodes.note: God appears again, repeats the new name, promises nations, kings, and land, and goes up from the place.
nodes.title: God confirms the name Israel at Bethel

nodes.note: Dinah is violated, Shechem seeks marriage, Jacob’s sons answer deceitfully, and Simeon and Levi kill the city’s males.
nodes.title: Violence brings shame upon Jacob’s household

nodes.note: Joseph reports on his brothers, receives a special garment, tells dreams, and is sent by Israel to seek the brothers’ welfare.
nodes.title: Israel sends Joseph to his brothers

nodes.note: Israel sacrifices at Beersheba, God addresses Jacob in night visions, and the household travels to Egypt.
nodes.title: Israel descends to Egypt after hearing God

nodes.note: The source names Jacob’s descendants by mothers, sons, daughters, and households and totals those entering Egypt.
nodes.title: A household is counted as the children of Israel

nodes.note: Israel claims Ephraim and Manasseh as his, crosses his hands, places the younger before the older, and blesses them.
nodes.title: Israel gives Joseph’s sons a place among his own

nodes.note: Jacob summons his sons, speaks distinct futures over them, and the narrator names them as the twelve tribes of Israel.
nodes.title: Israel speaks over the tribes before his death

pivots.title: A name becomes a people

pivots.description: Israel multiplies under pressure, is named God’s firstborn, leaves Egypt, crosses the sea, and sings after deliverance.

nodes.note: A family list opens into a numerous people, a new king fears them, and forced labor and death orders intensify.
nodes.title: The children of Israel multiply under oppression

nodes.note: The children of Israel groan, cry, and sigh under bondage.
nodes.title: God hears Israel and remembers covenant

nodes.note: The LORD says Israel’s affliction is seen and its cry heard, promises descent and deliverance, and sends Moses to Pharaoh.
nodes.title: Israel’s affliction leads to Moses’ commission

nodes.note: The LORD tells Moses what to say to Pharaoh and names Israel as son and firstborn.
nodes.title: Israel is called God’s son and firstborn

nodes.note: Israelite households mark doors with blood and remain inside while Egypt’s firstborn die.
nodes.title: Marked Israelite houses are passed over

nodes.note: The Egyptians urge departure, the people carry unleavened dough and requested goods, and a mixed multitude goes with them.
nodes.title: Israel leaves Egypt with a mixed company

nodes.note: Israel cries out at the approaching army, Moses calls for stillness, the sea opens, and the people cross on dry ground.
nodes.title: Israel fears, crosses, and sees Egypt defeated

nodes.note: Moses and the children of Israel sing of the LORD’s triumph, power, holiness, guidance, and future sanctuary.
nodes.title: Israel sings after the sea

pivots.title: A people under Egypt

pivots.description: Food, direct speech, covenant blood, rebellion, renewal, and glory shape Israel near Sinai.

nodes.note: The congregation complains about hunger, the LORD promises bread, and manna appears with instructions for daily gathering.
nodes.title: Israel receives bread and a daily test

nodes.note: At Sinai the LORD recalls carrying Israel from Egypt and proposes covenant obedience, treasured possession, priestly kingdom, and holy nation.
nodes.title: Israel is called a treasured possession and priestly kingdom

nodes.note: God speaks words concerning worship, name, Sabbath, family, life, marriage, property, testimony, and desire.
nodes.title: Israel hears the covenant words and stands far off

nodes.note: Moses records the words, the people twice promise obedience, blood is placed on altar and people, and representatives ascend, see Israel’s God, and eat and drink.
nodes.title: Israel enters covenant through words, blood, and a meal

nodes.note: The people demand gods, Aaron makes a calf, and the celebration names it as the one that brought Israel from Egypt.
nodes.title: Israel makes a calf while Moses is on the mountain

nodes.note: Moses breaks the tablets, destroys the calf, confronts Aaron, and the Levites kill within the camp.
nodes.title: Broken tablets, violence, and intercession follow the calf

nodes.note: Moses cuts new tablets, the LORD descends and proclaims mercy, grace, patience, covenant love, forgiveness, and judgment.
nodes.title: Covenant renewal begins with the divine name

nodes.note: The cloud covers the tent, glory fills the tabernacle, and even Moses cannot enter.
nodes.title: Glory fills the dwelling and guides Israel

pivots.title: Covenant at the mountain

pivots.description: Atonement, neighbor love, land, blessing, shared Spirit, fear, rebellion, and failed leadership define communal life.

nodes.note: After the deaths of Aaron’s sons, guarded entry, sacrifices, blood, confession, and the live goat address impurity and sin.
nodes.title: Atonement cleanses people, priests, and sanctuary

nodes.note: The whole congregation is told to be holy through family honor, Sabbath, worship, provision for poor and foreigner, honest judgment, truthful speech, and love of neighbor.
nodes.title: Holiness reaches fields, courts, speech, and neighbors

nodes.note: The land receives Sabbath, liberty is proclaimed in the jubilee, property returns, and prices reflect remaining years.
nodes.title: Israel’s land rests and returns

nodes.note: Aaron and his sons are given words of blessing for the children of Israel, naming protection, favor, grace, attention, and peace.
nodes.title: The divine name is placed on Israel in blessing

nodes.note: Craving and lament overwhelm Moses, who asks why he carries the people alone.
nodes.title: Complaint leads to shared leadership and Spirit

nodes.note: The spies agree that the land is fruitful but divide over whether Israel can enter.
nodes.title: The assembly chooses fear after seeing the land

nodes.note: The LORD threatens destruction, Moses appeals to reputation and proclaimed character, and the people are pardoned.
nodes.title: Pardon does not remove the wilderness sentence

nodes.note: The congregation disputes with Moses and Aaron, the LORD gives instructions, and water comes from the rock.
nodes.title: Israel receives water while leaders fail to honor God

pivots.title: A holy and difficult community

pivots.description: Judgment, blessing, compromise, inheritance, election, love, covenant, and return are rehearsed before entry.

nodes.note: Impatience becomes accusation, fiery serpents bring death, and the people confess and ask for intercession.

nodes.note: Balak builds altars and Balaam seeks a word, but the oracle asks how one can curse whom God has not cursed.
nodes.title: A hired curse becomes blessing over Israel

nodes.note: Sexual relations, sacrificial meals, and attachment to Baal bring anger and death.
nodes.title: Israel joins Baal of Peor and faces plague

nodes.note: Five women name their father, his death, lack of sons, and risk of losing his name.
nodes.title: The daughters of Zelophehad change Israel’s inheritance law

nodes.note: Moses calls Israel to hear and live, recalls Baal Peor, and says faithful practice will appear as wisdom to other peoples.
nodes.title: Israel’s life and law are displayed before nations

nodes.note: Israel is commanded to hear, love the LORD with the whole self, keep words in the heart, teach children, and mark ordinary spaces and routines.

nodes.note: Israel is called holy and treasured, but election is explicitly denied a basis in size.
nodes.title: Israel is chosen despite being few

nodes.title: Covenant includes hidden things, exile, return, and choice

nodes.note: Moses calls heaven and earth to hear a song that names God faithful, Israel corrupt, election unearned, apostasy foreseeable, and judgment severe.
nodes.title: Moses gives Israel a song that will testify against them

pivots.title: Identity before the land

pivots.description: Crossing, covenant, corporate guilt, repeated rescue, uneven participation, atrocity, and civil fracture test tribal solidarity.

nodes.note: The ark goes before the people, the waters stop, priests stand in the riverbed, and all Israel crosses.
nodes.title: All Israel crosses the Jordan on dry ground

nodes.note: Joshua recounts ancestors, exodus, wilderness, land, and defeated kings, then calls for exclusive service.
nodes.title: Israel rehearses its story and chooses whom to serve

nodes.title: A generation forgets and a cycle begins

nodes.note: David brings the ark with sacrifice, dancing, shouting, and trumpet, blesses the people, and distributes food.
nodes.title: David brings the ark into Jerusalem with celebration

nodes.note: At the Temple Solomon names covenant, sin, defeat, drought, famine, foreign prayer, war, captivity, forgiveness, justice, and return.
nodes.title: Solomon prays for Israel, foreigners, and future exiles

pivots.title: Israel asks for a king

pivots.description: The royal split, rival worship, prophetic contest, conquest, reform, and exile expose competing uses of Israel’s name.

nodes.title: The kingdom divides after Rehoboam answers harshly

nodes.note: Fearing return to David’s house, Jeroboam builds calves at Bethel and Dan, changes priesthood and festival, and presents the images as the gods who brought Israel from Egypt.

nodes.note: Ahab gathers Israel and Baal’s prophets, Elijah demands a choice, two sacrifices are prepared, and fire answers Elijah’s prayer.
nodes.title: Elijah asks Israel how long it will limp between claims

nodes.note: Samaria is captured and Israel exiled, and the narrator reviews idolatry, rejected warnings, covenant breach, imitation of nations, and child sacrifice.
nodes.title: The northern kingdom falls after a long indictment

nodes.note: Hezekiah removes high places and the bronze serpent, trusts the LORD, and prospers.

nodes.title: Josiah gathers Judah and Israel’s remnant for covenant renewal

nodes.note: Zedekiah rebels, Babylon besieges Jerusalem, famine intensifies, the king is captured, sons are killed, eyes are put out, Temple and city are burned, and people are exiled.
nodes.title: Judah falls and Jerusalem is emptied

pivots.description: Prophets address rebellion, election, justice, childhood, comfort, witness, false security, renewed covenant, and a cleansed name.

nodes.title: The servant called Israel is sent to restore Israel

nodes.note: Jeremiah stands at the Temple gate, rejects repeated trust in the building, demands justice and an end to oppression and idolatry, and points to Shiloh.

nodes.note: The LORD promises to be God of all Israel’s families, rebuild the virgin of Israel, bring a remnant from north and ends of earth, and lead them with weeping.
nodes.title: Scattered Israel is gathered with Ephraim at the center

nodes.note: The LORD promises sowing, rebuilding, individual accountability, a new covenant unlike the exodus covenant, instruction within, universal knowing, forgiveness, and enduring national identity under cosmic order.
nodes.title: A new covenant is promised to Israel and Judah

nodes.note: Hosea’s children receive names announcing an end to Jehu’s house, no mercy, and not my people.
nodes.title: Children bear names of judgment and future reunion

nodes.note: Elders come to inquire, but the prophetic speech retells rebellion in Egypt, wilderness, and land, repeatedly saying action was taken for the divine name.

nodes.note: Amos addresses the whole family brought from Egypt and says, “You only have I chosen,” therefore punishment follows.

pivots.description: Dry bones, reunited sticks, confession, return, communal memory, praise, and restored nations revisit Israel after catastrophe.

nodes.note: Daniel prays with fasting, confesses in the first-person plural, names covenant mercy and persistent disobedience, recalls the exodus, and asks for anger to turn from Jerusalem.
nodes.title: Daniel confesses Israel’s sin while asking for Jerusalem

nodes.note: Cyrus says the God of heaven charged him to build in Jerusalem, permits the people to go, neighbors contribute, and vessels taken by Nebuchadnezzar are counted and returned.
nodes.title: A foreign king authorizes return and restores Temple vessels

nodes.note: Ezra falls with torn garments, speaks of guilt rising to heaven, recalls brief favor and surviving remnant, and names present marriage trespass.
nodes.title: Ezra carries communal shame into confession

nodes.note: The assembly blesses God, recounts Abraham, Egypt, Sinai, wilderness, conquest, judges, kings, prophets, exile, and present servitude, and makes a written covenant.
nodes.title: Returned Israel retells creation, exodus, land, rebellion, and mercy

nodes.note: The psalm commands transmission to children, recalls Ephraim, exodus signs, wilderness testing, provision, repeated unbelief, sanctuary loss, Judah’s election, and David’s shepherding.
nodes.title: A teaching psalm narrates Israel’s failure and divine persistence

nodes.note: The psalm calls Abraham’s offspring and Jacob’s children to remember covenant, then follows ancestors, Joseph, Egypt, plagues, departure, wilderness provision, and land gift.
nodes.title: Israel remembers promise through providence and exodus

nodes.note: Praise opens into corporate confession covering the sea, craving, calf, spies, Peor, Meribah, land compromise, and exile.
nodes.title: Israel confesses repeated rebellion while asking to be gathered

nodes.note: The LORD promises return to Zion, old and young in safe streets, gathered remnant, renewed crops, truth and justice, transformed fasts, and nations seeking the LORD by taking hold of a Jew’s garment.
nodes.title: Restored Jerusalem draws many peoples toward Israel’s God

pivots.title: Exile, memory, and return

pivots.description: Later witnesses retell origins, confess failure, resist coercion, endure violence, and dispute Israel’s place among the nations.

nodes.note: Achior recounts Chaldean ancestry, departure, Egypt, exodus, wilderness, land, Temple, exile, and return, and warns that Israel is vulnerable when it sins but protected when faithful.
nodes.title: A foreign commander retells Israel’s story to an empire

nodes.note: The prayer names righteousness belonging to the Lord and shame to Judah, Jerusalem, kings, priests, prophets, ancestors, and people, recalls Egypt and covenant warnings, and asks mercy under foreign rule.
nodes.title: Exiled Israel confesses a long refusal to listen

nodes.note: The king commands one people, suppresses sacrifices, Sabbaths, feasts, circumcision, and law, and installs profaning worship.
nodes.title: Imperial policy tries to erase Israel’s practices

nodes.note: Officials invite Mattathias to lead compliance, but he declares loyalty to ancestral covenant, kills an apostate and royal officer, tears down the altar, and flees with family.
nodes.title: Mattathias rejects the king’s command and begins resistance

nodes.note: The brothers refuse prohibited food, speak of law, creation, resurrection, judgment, and restoration, and die under torture while their mother exhorts them.
nodes.title: A mother and seven sons resist torture

nodes.note: The king’s plan for elephants and death is repeatedly interrupted by sleep, confusion, and timing, while the Jews pray and wait.
nodes.title: Israelites face an ordered mass killing that is delayed

nodes.note: The mother addresses her children through birth, law, endurance, and ancestry and says no seducer corrupted her.
nodes.title: A mother identifies herself and her sons as Israelites

nodes.note: A prayer recalls creation, Adam’s rule, descent, and Israel’s inheritance, then contrasts Israel with nations said to be nothing.
nodes.title: Israel’s speaker claims the world while living dispossessed

nodes.note: Tobit blesses God as king, calls Israel to confess among nations, names scattering for wrongdoing and future gathering through mercy, and imagines rebuilt Jerusalem drawing nations.
nodes.title: A diaspora song joins discipline, mercy, gathering, and Jerusalem

pivots.title: Israel remembered under later empires

pivots.description: Gospel witnesses place Jesus amid Israel’s mercy, consolation, tribes, lost sheep, outsiders, judgment, and an Israelite named without deceit.

nodes.note: Mary’s song moves from personal lowliness to divine reversals, help for Israel, mercy, and the promise to Abraham and offspring.
nodes.title: Mary sings of mercy remembered toward Israel

nodes.note: Simeon waits for Israel’s consolation, receives the Spirit’s promise, and calls the child salvation, light for nations, and glory of Israel.
nodes.title: Simeon and Anna wait for Israel’s consolation and Jerusalem’s redemption

nodes.note: Flight to Egypt, return, slaughter, Rachel’s weeping, and settlement in Nazareth are linked to prophetic texts.
nodes.title: Jesus’ childhood is narrated through Israel’s Scripture

nodes.note: Jesus restricts the initial mission away from Gentiles and Samaritans, directs it to lost sheep of Israel, and sends proclamation, healing, dependence, warning, and endurance.
nodes.title: The Twelve are sent first to Israel’s lost sheep

nodes.note: A woman calls Jesus Son of David and asks mercy, the disciples seek dismissal, and Jesus names the lost sheep of Israel and children’s bread.
nodes.title: A Canaanite woman presses against Israel’s mission boundary

nodes.note: After the rich man departs, Jesus speaks of difficulty, divine possibility, renewal, twelve thrones, twelve tribes, relinquished households, and reversal of first and last.
nodes.title: The Twelve are promised judgment over Israel’s tribes

nodes.note: Tenants beat servants and kill the son, the audience names their own judgment, and Jesus applies rejected-stone Scripture and says the kingdom will be given to a nation producing fruit.
nodes.title: A vineyard parable brings leaders under judgment

nodes.note: Two disciples recount Jesus’ deeds, execution, their hope for Israel’s redemption, women’s report of an empty tomb, and the third day.
nodes.title: Disciples speak of their hope that Jesus would redeem Israel

nodes.note: Philip names Jesus through Moses and prophets, Nathanael questions Nazareth, and Jesus calls him an Israelite indeed without deceit.
nodes.title: Jesus calls Nathanael an Israelite without deceit

pivots.title: Jesus within Israel’s story

pivots.description: Acts, letters, and Revelation revisit ancestry, remnant, covenant, identity, inclusion, warning, worship, and the twelve tribes.

nodes.note: After resurrection teaching about God’s Kingdom, the disciples ask whether the kingdom will now be restored to Israel.
nodes.title: The disciples ask about restoring the kingdom to Israel

nodes.note: Peter calls Jesus a man attested by God, names human killing and divine resurrection, applies Davidic Psalms, and tells all Israel that God made Jesus Lord and Christ.
nodes.title: Peter addresses Israel with resurrection and repentance

nodes.note: Paul addresses men of Israel and God-fearers, recounts election, Egypt, wilderness, land, judges, Saul, David, John, Jesus, Jerusalem’s rejection, resurrection, promise, forgiveness, and warning.
nodes.title: Paul retells Israel’s history toward Jesus

nodes.note: Paul matches opponents’ ancestry claims and then subverts boasting through labor, suffering, anxiety for churches, weakness, and escape in a basket.
nodes.title: Paul names himself Hebrew, Israelite, and Abraham’s offspring

nodes.note: Paul names kinship, adoption, glory, covenants, law, service, promises, ancestors, and Christ, then says not all from Israel are Israel and develops the argument through Isaac, Jacob, Esau, mercy, and hardening.
nodes.title: Paul grieves for Israel and distinguishes Israel within Israel

nodes.note: Paul denies that God rejected the people, names himself an Israelite, recalls a remnant, warns Gentile branches against pride, anticipates fullness and “all Israel,” and concludes that all are shut up in disobedience for mercy.
nodes.title: Israel is discussed through remnant, branches, jealousy, and mercy

nodes.note: Paul contrasts circumcision boasting with the cross and says circumcision and uncircumcision are nothing but new creation, then speaks peace and mercy upon those walking by this rule and upon the Israel of God.
nodes.title: Paul closes with new creation and the Israel of God

nodes.note: Gentile readers are told they were once excluded from Messiah, alienated from Israel’s commonwealth, and strangers to covenants.
nodes.title: Former outsiders are brought near to Israel’s commonwealth

nodes.note: Paul lists circumcision, Israelite ancestry, Benjamin, Hebrew identity, law, zeal, and blamelessness as grounds for confidence in flesh.
nodes.title: Paul counts Israelite credentials as loss because of Christ

nodes.note: The letter contrasts covenants, quotes the promise to house of Israel and house of Judah, retains law, knowing God, forgiveness, and fault with the people, and calls the first covenant old and nearing disappearance.
nodes.title: Hebrews applies Jeremiah’s new covenant to its audience

nodes.note: Readers come to the rejected living stone and are called living stones, spiritual house, holy priesthood, chosen race, royal priesthood, holy nation, and God’s people.
nodes.title: A letter applies priestly and people language to its readers

nodes.note: The vision hears 144,000 sealed from named tribes of Israel and then sees a multitude from every nation before the throne and Lamb.
nodes.title: Sealed tribes stand beside an innumerable multitude

nodes.note: The bride-city descends with divine glory, twelve gates bear names of Israel’s tribes, foundations bear apostles’ names, no Temple is present, nations walk by its light, and nothing unclean enters.
nodes.title: Israel’s tribes name the gates of the New Jerusalem

pivots.title: Israel in apostolic argument and final vision

topic.trailPrompt: Notice who is called Israel, who speaks for the people, what binds or divides them, how their past is retold, which outsiders are present, and what each source leaves unresolved about belonging.
